questions.question: What is the primary architectural purpose of a distributed version control system (DVCS) like Git?
options: A central server stores all code and clients only keep lightweight metadata pointers
It eliminates the need for branches by overwriting files immediately in real time
Source code is compiled directly on a central mainframe before distribution to developers
Every developer clone contains the entire project history and repository mirror locally
questions.explanation: In Git's distributed architecture, every local clone is a full repository backup containing complete commit history, enabling offline operations and decentralized workflows.

questions.question: Which three distinct zones constitute the core local architecture of Git?
options: Feature Branch, Release Tag, and Master Mirror
Working Directory, Staging Area (Index), and Repository (HEAD)
Frontend UI, Backend Controller, and SQL Database
RAM, ROM, and Solid State Drive
questions.explanation: Git manages local changes across three distinct areas: the Working Directory (modified files), the Staging Area / Index (prepared snapshot), and the Repository (committed history in HEAD).

questions.question: What fundamental data structure does Git use internally to represent commit history and object relationships?
options: Singly Linked List with integer auto-incrementing IDs
Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of cryptographically hashed objects
B+ Tree indexed table stored in SQLite
Circular FIFO buffer allocated in cache memory
questions.explanation: Git models commits, trees, and blobs as immutable objects in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), linked together by their SHA-1 cryptographic hashes.

questions.question: In Git object storage, what is a 'blob' (Binary Large Object) responsible for storing?
options: The folder directory hierarchy and file permissions
The active branch pointers and remote URLs
The commit author name, email, and timestamp only
The pure file contents/data without filename or directory metadata
questions.explanation: A blob stores solely raw file contents. Directory structures, filenames, and file modes are stored in 'tree' objects.

questions.question: What is the function of the HEAD pointer in a Git repository?
options: It marks the very first root commit created during repository initialization
It specifies the HTTPS URL of the remote GitHub repository
It points to the current branch reference or the latest commit in your active working tree
It locks files against concurrent edits across the network
questions.explanation: HEAD is a symbolic reference indicating which commit or branch is currently checked out in your local working directory.

questions.question: What scenario causes Git to enter a 'detached HEAD' state?
options: When the local hard drive runs out of disk space during a merge
When two developers commit simultaneously with identical timestamps
Checking out a specific commit SHA, tag, or remote branch directly rather than a local named branch
When the remote GitHub server fails to respond to SSH handshakes
questions.explanation: A detached HEAD occurs when HEAD points directly to a commit SHA rather than a branch ref. Commits made in this state can be lost if not attached to a named branch before switching away.

questions.question: What is the exact purpose of the .gitignore file?
options: To hide sensitive code lines from developers during peer reviews
To define file patterns that Git should intentionally ignore from tracking and staging
To bypass password requirements when pushing to remote servers
To permanently delete binary files from the local file system upon commit
questions.explanation: .gitignore prevents unintended files (such as build artifacts, node_modules, .env secrets, and log files) from being tracked by Git.

questions.question: How does Git guarantee the cryptographic integrity of its object database?
options: By signing every file with a hardware TPM security chip
By using operating system file locking mechanisms
By storing duplicate files across hidden cloud partitions
Every object is addressed and verified by its SHA-1 / SHA-256 content hash
questions.explanation: Git uses content-addressable storage where the identity of any object is the hash of its contents. Modifying even one byte changes the hash and breaks the commit chain.

questions.question: What is stored inside the hidden .git folder in your project root?
options: The entire object database, commit history, refs, configuration, hooks, and staging index
The operating system virtual machine hypervisor configuration
Only compiled binary bytecode and node dependency caches
Temporary scratch files that can be deleted safely at any time
questions.explanation: The `.git` directory contains the complete Git repository engine—including refs, objects, index, config, and commit history.

questions.question: Which command creates a brand new Git repository in your current working folder?
options: git start
git setup
git init
git create
questions.explanation: `git init` creates the `.git` directory and initializes all core metadata structures needed for version tracking.

questions.question: What distinguishes Git from Centralized Version Control Systems (CVCS) like SVN or TFS?
options: Git allows full offline commits, branching, and history inspection without connecting to a central server
Git does not support branching or merging workflows
Git requires constant 24/7 internet connectivity to record file changes
CVCS stores all repositories in local developer RAM while Git uses tape storage
questions.explanation: CVCS requires a continuous connection to a central server for commits and history queries, whereas Git performs virtually all operations locally and instantaneously.

questions.question: Which glob pattern in .gitignore recursively ignores all .env files across the entire project repository?
options: /env-all
ignore .env
*.env
.env::all
questions.explanation: The glob pattern `*.env` matches and ignores any file ending with `.env` in the root directory or any nested subdirectory.

questions.question: What is a 'tree' object in Git's internal architecture?
options: A visualization tool used exclusively in graphical Git user interfaces
A security certificate authorizing SSH connections
An object that represents a directory, mapping filenames to blob SHA hashes and sub-trees
A data compression algorithm used to zip repository downloads
questions.explanation: A tree object corresponds to a directory entry in the filesystem, associating filenames, modes, and SHA hashes of blobs and child trees.

questions.question: What metadata is permanently recorded inside a Git 'commit' object?
options: The full source code of the operating system and BIOS version
Tree hash, parent commit hash(es), author, committer, timestamps, and commit message
The user's GitHub billing account details
The IP addresses of all computers that downloaded the repository
questions.explanation: A commit object captures the top-level tree hash (snapshot of project files), parent commit SHA pointers, author/committer credentials, timestamps, and the log message.

questions.question: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
options: Git and GitHub are identical open-source desktop software packages
Git is a paid enterprise database; GitHub is an open-source text editor
Git is developed for Windows operating systems; GitHub is exclusively for Linux
Git is the version control CLI tool; GitHub is a cloud-based hosting and collaboration platform for Git repositories
questions.explanation: Git is the distributed version control system tool itself. GitHub is an online service that hosts Git repositories and provides pull requests, issues, and CI/CD pipelines.

questions.question: Which command sets your global author email across all Git repositories on your system?
options: git set --email "you@example.com"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git auth --user-email "you@example.com"
git register-email "you@example.com"
questions.explanation: `git config --global user.email "..."` writes your author email to the global `~/.gitconfig` configuration file.

questions.question: What state is a file in after it has been modified in the working directory but not yet staged?
options: Modified (Unstaged)
Committed
Staged
Untracked (New)
questions.explanation: A previously tracked file that contains local edits is in the 'Modified' (unstaged) state until `git add` moves it to the 'Staged' state.

questions.question: What happens when you run git status on a freshly cloned, clean repository?
options: It forces a remote fetch and rebases the current branch
It prints a fatal error requiring repository re-initialization
It reports 'nothing to commit, working tree clean'
It deletes all untracked files automatically
questions.explanation: When no files are modified, staged, or untracked relative to the HEAD commit, `git status` confirms the working tree is clean.

questions.question: Why does Git store file changes as full snapshots rather than delta difference lists?
options: Because snapshots consume zero hard drive storage space
Because Git cannot compute differences between files
Because delta storage is forbidden by open-source licenses
Snapshots allow rapid branch switching and cryptographic integrity verification without recalculating deltas
questions.explanation: Git treats data as a stream of snapshots over time. While packfiles compress identical blobs later, the conceptual snapshot model makes checkouts and history traversal extremely fast.

questions.question: Which command displays the configured Git configuration settings and where they originate?
options: git config --list --show-origin
git inspect-config
git show-config --all
git view --settings
questions.explanation: `git config --list --show-origin` outputs all effective configuration keys alongside the exact file paths (system, global, local) where they are defined.

lessons.lessonTitle: Core Git Commands: init, add, commit, push, pull

questions.question: Which command moves all modified and newly created untracked files in the current folder to the staging area?
options: git push --all
git commit --stage
git stage --all-now
git add .
questions.explanation: `git add .` stages all modifications and new untracked files in the current working directory and subdirectories into the index.

questions.question: What is the correct syntax to create a commit with an inline descriptive message?
options: git commit --message = "Descriptive commit message"
git record -msg "Descriptive commit message"
git commit -m "Descriptive commit message"
git save -m "Descriptive commit message"
questions.explanation: `git commit -m "message"` records a snapshot of the staged changes with the provided inline log message.

questions.question: What does the command git diff without flags display?
options: A summary list of all commit hashes created in the last 24 hours
Differences between your working directory and the staging area (unstaged changes)
Differences between your local branch and the remote origin master branch
Differences between the staging area and the latest commit in HEAD
questions.explanation: By default, `git diff` shows the unstaged changes currently in your working directory compared to the staging index.

questions.question: Which command compares changes that are currently staged in the index against the last commit in HEAD?
options: git diff --index-all
git diff --staged (or git diff --cached)
git diff --head-only
git diff --ready
questions.explanation: `git diff --staged` (synonym `--cached`) displays the exact diff of changes that have been added to the staging area and will be included in the next commit.

questions.question: How can you stage and commit all modified tracked files in a single shortcut command?
options: git push --commit "Commit message"
git add --commit "Commit message"
git commit -all -save "Commit message"
git commit -am "Commit message"
questions.explanation: `git commit -am "..."` automatically stages all tracked modified files (not untracked files) and commits them in a single step.

questions.question: What does git log --oneline --graph --decorate achieve?
options: A concise, visual ASCII graph of commit history, branches, and tags with one line per commit
A graphical popup window displaying source code syntax highlighting
An automated rollback of the last five commits in history
A direct export of the repository to a PDF report
questions.explanation: `--oneline` truncates commit hashes and shows one line per commit, `--graph` draws an ASCII branch merge graph, and `--decorate` shows branch and tag pointers.

questions.question: Which command connects your local repository to a remote repository hosted on GitHub?
options: git remote add origin https://github.com/user/repo.git
git remote set-url new https://github.com/user/repo.git
git connect origin https://github.com/user/repo.git
git link --remote https://github.com/user/repo.git
questions.explanation: `git remote add <name> <url>` registers a new remote repository alias (conventionally named `origin`).

questions.question: What does the -u (or --set-upstream) flag do when running git push -u origin main?
options: It unzips compressed files on the remote server
It pushes the branch and links local main to track remote origin/main for future parameterless pushes
It undoes the previous commit before pushing new files
It unlocks the remote repository for public read access
questions.explanation: The `-u` flag sets the default upstream tracking reference so subsequent pushes and pulls can simply use `git push` or `git pull`.

questions.question: What is the key difference between git fetch and git pull?
options: git fetch deletes local files; git pull restores them from the trash
git fetch downloads remote commits without merging; git pull fetches remote commits and automatically merges them into the active branch
git fetch is an alias for git clone; git pull is an alias for git push
git fetch works with GitHub; git pull only works with GitLab
questions.explanation: `git fetch` safely updates remote tracking branches (`origin/main`) without modifying your local working files. `git pull` is essentially `git fetch` followed by `git merge`.

questions.question: Which command un-stages a file from the staging area while preserving your modifications in the working directory?
options: git delete --staged <file>
git remove --keep <file>
git revert --soft <file>
git restore --staged <file> (or git reset HEAD <file>)
questions.explanation: `git restore --staged <file>` removes the specified file from the staging area without discarding local modifications in your working directory.

questions.question: How can you safely modify the commit message of the most recent commit before pushing?
options: git revert HEAD --edit "Updated commit message"
git update-message "Updated commit message"
git commit --fix-last "Updated commit message"
git commit --amend -m "Updated commit message"
questions.explanation: `git commit --amend` replaces the tip of the current branch with a new commit incorporating any staged changes and/or an updated commit message.

questions.question: Which command completely discards unstaged local modifications in a specific file, reverting it to the HEAD version?
options: git clean -f <file>
git rollback <file>
git restore <file> (or git checkout -- <file>)
git drop <file>
questions.explanation: `git restore <file>` overwrites working tree changes with the version from the staging area or HEAD, permanently discarding uncommitted local edits.

questions.question: What command removes untracked files and directories from the working tree that are not ignored by .gitignore?
options: git clear -untracked
git purge --all
git rm --untracked
git clean -fd
questions.explanation: `git clean -f` forces the deletion of untracked files, and `-d` includes untracked directories.

questions.question: Which command lists all configured remote repository names and their fetch/push URLs?
options: git remotes --show
git remote -v
git remote --list-all
git view --remotes
questions.explanation: `git remote -v` (verbose) outputs the names and corresponding fetch and push URLs for all registered remote repositories.

questions.question: What does git clone <url> do when executed in an empty directory?
options: It deploys the application directly to a live web server
It downloads the remote repository, initializes .git, checks out the default branch, and configures origin
It creates a shallow zip archive without commit history
It copies code to the clipboard without saving files to disk
questions.explanation: `git clone` initializes a new local directory, copies the entire remote repository and history, sets up remote tracking branches, and checks out the default branch.

questions.question: Which command shows the line-by-line author attribution and commit SHA for a specific file?
options: git authors <file>
git audit <file>
git blame <file>
git who <file>
questions.explanation: `git blame <file>` annotates each line of a file with the commit hash, author, and date of the last modification.

questions.question: How do you inspect the full details, diff, and metadata of a specific commit SHA?
options: git view-commit <commit-sha>
git log --commit=<commit-sha>
git show <commit-sha>
git inspect <commit-sha>
questions.explanation: `git show <commit-sha>` displays the commit metadata, author information, log message, and the unified diff of changes introduced by that commit.

questions.question: What does git rm <file> do compared to deleting the file using standard OS commands?
options: It deletes the file from the filesystem and stages the deletion in Git index automatically
It deletes the file from remote GitHub but keeps it locally
It creates a backup copy of the file in the root directory
It encrypts the file so other developers cannot read it
questions.explanation: `git rm <file>` removes the file from both the working directory and stages the removal in the index, ready for the next commit.

questions.question: Which command limits the output of git log to the 5 most recent commits?
options: git log --top 5
git log -n 5 (or git log -5)
git log --limit 5
git log --count 5
questions.explanation: `git log -n 5` or `git log -5` limits the commit history output to the specified number of recent commits.

questions.question: What happens when you run git push origin main and remote main contains commits you do not have locally?
options: Git automatically deletes all remote commits to prioritize your local code
Git creates a duplicate hidden repository on GitHub
Git crashes the remote GitHub server
Git rejects the push with a non-fast-forward error, requiring you to pull/merge remote updates first
questions.explanation: Git enforces non-fast-forward protection. You must fetch and integrate remote changes (`git pull`) before your push will be accepted.

questions.question: What is a branch in Git from an architectural standpoint?
options: A physical hardware partition on the developer's storage drive
A database table containing locked rows
A complete duplicate copy of all project files in a separate folder
A lightweight, movable pointer (40-byte file) referencing a specific commit SHA
questions.explanation: In Git, a branch is merely a lightweight pointer containing the 40-character SHA of its latest commit. Creating a branch is virtually instantaneous and consumes only 41 bytes.

questions.question: Which modern Git command creates a new branch named feature-login and switches to it immediately?
options: git move -b feature-login
git branch --create-and-move feature-login
git switch -c feature-login (or git checkout -b feature-login)
git new-branch feature-login
questions.explanation: `git switch -c <name>` (introduced in Git 2.23) or `git checkout -b <name>` creates a new branch and checks it out simultaneously.

questions.question: Which command lists all local and remote branches in the repository?
options: git list --branches
git view-branches -v
git branch -a
git branch --show-all-remotes
questions.explanation: `git branch -a` (all) lists both local branches and remote-tracking branches (prefixed with `remotes/origin/`).

questions.question: What is a 'Fast-Forward' merge in Git?
options: A merge executed using multiple CPU threads simultaneously
A merge that forces remote repository overwrites without checking conflicts
A merge where the target branch pointer is simply advanced directly forward to the source commit without creating a merge commit
A merge that skips automated tests to complete faster
questions.explanation: A fast-forward merge occurs when no divergent commits exist on the base branch; Git simply moves the base branch pointer forward to match the feature branch.

questions.question: Which flag forces Git to create a dedicated merge commit even if a fast-forward merge is possible?
options: git merge --force-commit <branch>
git merge --create-node <branch>
git merge --always-commit <branch>
git merge --no-ff <branch>
questions.explanation: `git merge --no-ff` preserves the historical existence of the feature branch in the graph by generating a merge commit even when fast-forward is possible.

questions.question: Under what exact condition does a Git merge conflict occur?
options: Whenever a merge involves more than 10 files simultaneously
Whenever code comments contain special punctuation characters
When developers commit from different operating systems (Windows vs macOS)
When two branches modify the exact same lines of the same file differently since their common ancestor
questions.explanation: Merge conflicts happen when Git encounters competing changes to the same lines of code in the same file and cannot automatically determine which version is correct.

questions.question: In a conflicted file, what does the marker <<<<<<< HEAD denote?
options: The code that will be automatically deleted by Git
A fatal syntax error reported by the compiler
The start of the incoming changes from the branch being merged
The beginning of the changes present in your currently checked-out active branch
questions.explanation: `<<<<<<< HEAD` marks the start of the code version from the current branch. `=======` separates the conflicting versions, and `>>>>>>> <branch>` marks the end of incoming changes.

questions.question: What are the correct steps to resolve and finalize a merge conflict?
options: Delete the repository and clone it again from GitHub
Run git push --force to override the conflict markers
Edit the conflicted file to resolve differences, remove conflict markers, run git add <file>, and execute git commit
Rename the file and delete the other branch immediately
questions.explanation: To resolve a conflict: manually edit the file to the desired state, remove the `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` markers, stage the resolved file (`git add`), and finalize with `git commit`.

questions.question: Which command aborts an ongoing merge and returns your working tree to the pre-merge state?
options: git stop-merge
git merge --abort
git rollback --merge
git merge --cancel
questions.explanation: `git merge --abort` halts the merge process and restores the working directory and HEAD to the state before `git merge` was executed.

questions.question: How do you safely delete a local branch that has already been merged into main?
options: git delete-branch <branch-name>
git remove-branch <branch-name>
git branch -d <branch-name>
git branch -D <branch-name>
questions.explanation: `git branch -d` (lowercase) deletes a branch only if it has been fully merged into its upstream, preventing accidental loss of unmerged work.

questions.question: Which command force-deletes a local branch containing unmerged changes?
options: git branch -force-del <branch-name>
git branch --kill <branch-name>
git branch -D <branch-name>
git drop-branch <branch-name>
questions.explanation: `git branch -D` (uppercase, shortcut for `--delete --force`) deletes a branch regardless of its merge status.

questions.question: How do you delete a remote branch named feature-cart from GitHub?
options: git remove origin/feature-cart
git push origin --delete feature-cart (or git push origin :feature-cart)
git delete remote feature-cart
git remote branch --delete feature-cart
questions.explanation: `git push origin --delete <branch>` sends a request to the remote server to delete the specified branch ref.

questions.question: What is the Gitflow branching model standard for staging and releasing production code?
options: main contains production releases, develop contains integrated features, and short-lived feature/* branches branch off develop
develop is deployed to production and main is used for testing
Every developer maintains a completely separate repository with no shared branches
All developers commit directly to main without creating branches
questions.explanation: Gitflow uses `main` for stable production releases, `develop` for integration, `feature/*` for new capabilities, `release/*` for pre-prod hardening, and `hotfix/*` for urgent patches.

questions.question: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
options: git rebase deletes all commit messages permanently while git merge preserves them
git rebase is an irreversible command that destroys code
git merge preserves complete history with a merge commit; git rebase re-applies commits on top of another base, creating a linear history
git merge is only for local branches; git rebase is only for GitHub
questions.explanation: `git merge` creates a new merge commit combining two histories. `git rebase` moves the base of your feature branch to the tip of target branch, rewriting commit SHAs to produce a clean linear history.

questions.question: Why should you avoid running git rebase on shared public branches (like main)?
options: Rebasing rewrites commit SHA hashes, which desynchronizes the commit history for all other collaborating developers
Because Git will automatically delete the repository from GitHub
Because GitHub forbids rebase operations on paid accounts
Because rebasing on public branches causes CPU hardware overheating
questions.explanation: The Golden Rule of Rebasing: Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a public/shared repository, as rewriting public history breaks tracking for team members.

questions.question: Which command allows you to temporarily shelve (stash) uncommitted modifications without committing them?
options: git stash
git pause
git temporary-save
git hold
questions.explanation: `git stash` saves your modified working directory and staged changes to a temporary storage stack and reverts your working tree to match the HEAD commit.

questions.question: How do you re-apply your most recently stashed changes and remove them from the stash stack?
options: git stash pop
git stash apply --clean
git stash restore
git stash extract
questions.explanation: `git stash pop` applies the modifications from the top of the stash stack (`stash@{0}`) back to your working directory and removes them from the stash list.

questions.question: Which command shows the list of all currently saved stash entries?
options: git stash --show-all
git stash view
git stash list
git list-stashes
questions.explanation: `git stash list` outputs all saved stash references (`stash@{0}`, `stash@{1}`, etc.) along with the branch and commit where they were created.

questions.question: What does git cherry-pick <commit-sha> do?
options: Applies the exact changes introduced by a specific commit from another branch onto your currently checked-out branch
Replaces the current branch with a random commit
Deletes a specific commit from history across all branches
Picks the top 5 highest rated commits on GitHub
questions.explanation: `git cherry-pick <commit-sha>` copies the diff of a specific existing commit and commits it cleanly onto the current branch as a new commit.

questions.question: Which command displays which branches contain a specific commit SHA?
options: git whereis <commit-sha>
git branch --contains <commit-sha>
git find-commit <commit-sha>
git branch --has <commit-sha>
questions.explanation: `git branch --contains <commit-sha>` lists all local branches that have the specified commit in their direct ancestor history.

questions.question: What is a Pull Request (PR) in modern software engineering workflows?
options: A mechanism to lock all developers out of a repository
A formal proposal on a platform like GitHub to review, discuss, and merge code changes from a feature branch into a target branch
A command that pulls binary dependencies from the npm registry
A request to purchase additional cloud server memory
questions.explanation: A Pull Request (or Merge Request in GitLab) is a collaborative review mechanism where developers submit code changes for automated testing, peer review, and approval before merging.

questions.question: In open-source workflows on GitHub, what is a 'Fork'?
options: A command that terminates a repository connection
A hardware server rack used to host Git repositories
A personal, independent copy of another user's repository hosted under your own GitHub account
A software tool used to split commit messages into multiple lines
questions.explanation: A Fork creates a distinct copy of an upstream repository under your GitHub account, allowing you to freely experiment and submit pull requests without write access to the original project.

questions.question: What is the standard convention for configuring remotes in a forked repository workflow?
options: origin points to your personal fork; upstream points to the original central repository
remote1 points to production; remote2 points to staging
origin points to the local folder; upstream points to Google Drive
master points to your fork; main points to the original repository
questions.explanation: Conventionally, `origin` references your personal fork on GitHub where you push feature branches, and `upstream` references the parent open-source project from which you pull upstream updates.

questions.question: How do you synchronize your local master branch with the latest changes from the original upstream repository?
options: git fetch upstream && git checkout main && git merge upstream/main
git push upstream main --force
git download upstream/main
git sync --all-remotes
questions.explanation: Syncing a fork requires fetching commits from the upstream remote (`git fetch upstream`) and merging `upstream/main` into your local `main` branch.

questions.question: What role do Branch Protection Rules play on GitHub?
options: They restrict repository access to a single computer IP address
They automatically delete branches after 7 days of inactivity
They enforce safeguards such as requiring peer PR approvals, passing CI checks, and preventing direct force-pushes to main
They encrypt repository files using user passwords
questions.explanation: Branch protection rules protect critical branches (like `main`) by requiring code reviews, passing CI/CD status checks, preventing deletions, and blocking direct `git push --force`.

questions.question: What is Continuous Integration (CI) in the context of GitHub Pull Requests?
options: An automated bot that answers student questions in chat
A billing system that charges for each line of code written
Automated pipelines that build, lint, and run test suites against every PR commit to detect bugs before merging
A system that automatically commits code every 5 minutes
questions.explanation: CI (e.g., GitHub Actions) automatically triggers automated test runners, linters, and security vulnerability scanners whenever code is pushed or a PR is opened.

questions.question: Which merge strategy on GitHub combines all commits in a PR into a single unified commit on the target branch?
options: Squash and Merge
Standard Create Merge Commit
Direct Mirror Push
Rebase and Fast-Forward
questions.explanation: 'Squash and Merge' condenses all individual WIP commits from the feature branch into a single clean commit with a consolidated message on the base branch.

questions.question: How does a developer leave an inline comment on a specific line of code during a GitHub PR review?
options: By committing a text file containing the feedback to the branch
By writing the comment inside .gitignore
By navigating to the 'Files changed' tab, hovering over the target code line, and clicking the '+' icon
By sending an email with the line number to the repository owner
questions.explanation: In GitHub's 'Files changed' diff viewer, reviewers click the '+' on any modified line to start an inline discussion thread, request changes, or suggest code replacements.

questions.question: What keyword in a PR description automatically closes linked issue #42 when the PR is merged into the default branch?
options: Link #42
Relates #42
See #42
Fixes #42 (or Closes #42, Resolves #42)
questions.explanation: GitHub recognizes keywords like `Closes #42`, `Fixes #42`, or `Resolves #42` in the PR body and automatically closes the referenced issue upon merging.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a README.md file in a GitHub repository?
options: It stores the billing history of the repository
It contains encrypted database passwords for production deployment
It instructs the Git compiler how to build binary executables
It serves as the landing page documentation explaining the project's purpose, setup instructions, usage, and architecture
questions.explanation: `README.md` is written in Markdown and renders automatically on the repository root page to guide developers on installation, prerequisites, and features.

questions.question: What file defines automated CI/CD workflows using GitHub Actions?
options: YAML files stored in the .github/workflows/ directory
XML files defined in public/workflows/
Python scripts located in ~/.git/actions/
JSON files stored in the root/config/ directory
questions.explanation: GitHub Actions automatically discovers and executes workflow pipelines defined as `.yml` or `.yaml` files inside `.github/workflows/`.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of using SSH keys rather than Personal Access Tokens for Git authentication?
options: Public-key cryptography provides secure, password-less authentication without exposing credentials in command history
SSH keys allow access to private repositories without owner permission
SSH keys increase download speeds by 500%
SSH keys eliminate the need to run git commit
questions.explanation: SSH keys (like ed25519) use asymmetric cryptography to authenticate your local machine securely and permanently with GitHub without re-entering tokens.

questions.question: What does a 'Draft Pull Request' indicate on GitHub?
options: Work is in progress and open for discussion, but not yet ready for formal review or merging
The PR has been permanently rejected by the maintainers
The PR has failed automated unit test validation
The PR can only be viewed by GitHub employees
questions.explanation: Draft PRs allow developers to share work-in-progress code and trigger CI pipelines while signaling to the team that the branch is not yet ready for final review.

questions.question: Which file format and location is used to provide an issue or PR template for contributors?
options: Text files in templates/git/
HTML files in public/templates/
Python files in backend/templates/
Markdown files in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/ or .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md
questions.explanation: Placing `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` or markdown files in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` pre-populates standardized contribution forms when developers open PRs or issues.

questions.question: How do you update an existing open Pull Request after making changes based on reviewer feedback?
options: Delete the remote branch and recreate it from scratch
Commit your changes locally and run git push origin <feature-branch>—the PR updates automatically
Close the current PR and open a brand new PR with the new code
Email the updated file attachments directly to the reviewer
questions.explanation: A Pull Request tracks the branch head. Pushing new commits to the remote feature branch automatically updates the PR diff, discussion timeline, and triggers CI checks.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the CODEOWNERS file in a repository?
options: It automatically assigns designated individuals or teams as mandatory reviewers when files they own are modified in a PR
It lists the copyright ownership and licensing terms of the codebase
It grants root access to server infrastructure
It restricts who can clone the repository from GitHub
questions.explanation: The `.github/CODEOWNERS` file defines patterns matching files and directories to specific GitHub users or teams who are automatically requested for review on relevant PRs.

questions.question: What does the GitHub 'Rebase and Merge' option do when merging a PR?
options: It deletes all commit authors and replaces them with the repository owner
It re-applies the PR commits individually on top of the base branch without a merge commit, maintaining individual commit granularity
It squashes all commits into a single commit
It creates an octopus merge with all historical branches
questions.explanation: 'Rebase and Merge' appends each individual commit from the PR branch onto the tip of the base branch linearly without creating a merge commit.

questions.question: Which command generates a new high-security Ed25519 SSH key pair on your machine?
options: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com"
ssh-auth --generate-key ed25519
github-keys generate --email "..."
git create-ssh --type ed25519
questions.explanation: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "email"` generates a modern, cryptographically secure Ed25519 SSH public/private key pair.

questions.question: What does a green checkmark next to a commit on GitHub signify?
options: The commit was created by an automated bot
The commit contains zero lines of code modifications
The commit was approved by GitHub legal compliance
All automated CI/CD checks, unit tests, and linters associated with the commit passed successfully
questions.explanation: Status badges (green checkmarks, yellow dots, or red crosses) reflect the live build and test results reported by CI/CD integrations like GitHub Actions.

questions.question: What is the ultimate professional outcome of enforcing structured Git collaboration workflows?
options: High code quality, regression prevention, clear audit trails, and seamless multi-developer team velocity
Preventing developers from writing Python code
Eliminating the need to write unit tests or documentation
Restricting code releases to once every five years
questions.explanation: Structured Git workflows with feature branches, code reviews, automated CI, and branch protection enable teams to deploy software rapidly and reliably with complete auditability.
